case_study_insert.main_stem: Northgate Logistics (NGL) is a private limited company in the distribution and courier sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2005 by Priya Raman, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. NGL plans to invest $840,000 in an automated warehouse sorting system and an electric van fleet, financed by a $480,000 five-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $17.50, and produces 75,000 units a year. NGL faces a parcel mis-sorting rate of 2.8% and rising damage complaints from online retailers. Priya Raman personally approves all capital spending, and the depot runs two shifts a day.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: NGL handled 75,000 consignments last year, up 12% on the previous year, but 2.8% were mis-sorted and 33 written complaints were received last month. On-time delivery is 93.5% against a 96% target, and average dispatch time is 4.6 hours from order to van. A survey of 350 e-commerce retailers found 66% would pay $0.55 more for guaranteed same-day delivery, and 58% rank damage-free handling first. Fourteen of the 55 warehouse staff need scanner training at $650 each. The warehouse return rate is 5.2%.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northgate Logistics (NGL) for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate has risen from 4.6% to 5.35%, raising the cost of variable-rate business loans. (2) Fuel and warehouse electricity prices have risen 2.4% year-on-year, only slightly above recent levels. (3) Consumer spending on online retail fell 7.8% in the latest quarter, while spending on in-store shopping rose 1.9%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for NGL of funding the $840,000 sorting system from retained profit rather than the $480,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit has no interest charge or instalments, preserving cash while the automated sorter is installed. The base rate has moved from 4.6% to 5.35%, so the $480,000 five-year bank loan is becoming dearer; the $360,000 retained profit is free. Each consignment earns $7.50 ($17.50 − $10.00), giving $562,500 of contribution at 75,000 consignments, which NGL can use to absorb the 2.8% mis-sorting cost without raising the $17.50 price.

Point 2: Equity funding avoids collateral and the risk of repossession if the new sorter fails to cut the 33 monthly complaints. No lender can impose conditions on Priya Raman's capital decisions, which suits her centralised, autocratic control of spending. Using retained profit also keeps the bank's credit headroom intact for a later van-fleet purchase, giving NGL flexibility if the 7.8% fall in online retail spending reduces the volume passing through the warehouse. The 12% growth in consignment volume recorded in Appendix 1 makes that internal cash especially valuable if the sorter needs further adjustment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Northgate Logistics (NGL), its sorting investment and its cost structure.

questions.question_text: Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or trade-magazine advertising. Which should NGL choose to promote same-day delivery to e-commerce retailers? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: Television would create wide awareness of NGL's same-day service and could impress the public, but the airtime cost is high for a 55-employee firm already funding an $840,000 sorter. Most viewers do not buy courier contracts, so the campaign would reach few of the 350 retailers in the survey.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper and quick to book, and it could cover NGL's depot catchment. However, e-commerce retailers buy nationally, and local listeners are largely consumers rather than business decision-makers; the reach is too narrow to fill the 75,000-consignment plan needed against $300,000 of fixed costs.

Trade-magazine advertising: Advertising in logistics and e-commerce publications reaches the purchasing managers who decide on carriers, matching the 350 retailers surveyed. It is far cheaper than television, can show the 93.5% on-time delivery record and the $0.55 same-day premium, and can be repeated in issues timed to peak seasons. Its weakness is long lead time and limited reach outside the trade.

Recommendation: NGL should choose trade-magazine advertising. It targets exactly the retailers who rank damage-free handling first, is affordable alongside the $480,000 loan, and supports the $0.55 premium. National television is rejected as costly and untargeted; local radio is rejected as too narrow and consumer-focused. NGL should follow up magazine leads with direct sales visits, since the 7.8% fall in online spending means contracts must be won actively. NGL can measure lead quality against the 350-retailer survey before renewing the campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to NGL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of NGL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of NGL with a justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for NGL of using autocratic leadership to tackle the 2.8% parcel mis-sorting rate.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Priya Raman issue clear, immediate instructions on scanner use and sorting routes, which suits a hierarchical structure with 55 warehouse staff. Decisive orders can cut the 2.8% mis-sorting rate quickly and help lift on-time delivery from 93.5% toward the 96% target, protecting the $17.50 price and the $7.50 contribution on each of 75,000 consignments.

Point 2: Central control speeds up investment decisions such as buying the scanners that the 14 staff need training on at $650 each, and enforces standard routines across shifts. This reduces the 33 written complaints and the 5.2% return rate, giving online retailers confidence in damage-free handling. The style has a cost — staff may feel little ownership of quality — so NGL should pair firm directives with feedback from sorters to sustain the improvement. Priya Raman can reinforce the message through the existing hierarchy without adding to the $300,000 fixed-cost base.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual analysis linked to NGL's sorting accuracy, complaints and investment decisions.

questions.question_text: Consider on-the-job scanner training for the 14 warehouse staff or external recruitment of experienced sorters. Which should NGL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job scanner training: Training the 14 staff on NGL's own scanners is directly relevant and avoids the $650 per-person course fee, so it is cheaper than hiring replacements. It keeps the 55-strong team intact and can be delivered during quieter periods, protecting the 75,000-consignment operation. The weakness is that trainers are working staff whose own duties suffer, and bad scanning habits may persist, which would leave the 2.8% mis-sorting rate unchanged.

External recruitment: Hiring experienced sorters brings fresh skills and could raise accuracy faster, supporting the 93.5% on-time target and reducing the 33 complaints. External candidates may challenge existing routines, but recruitment and induction costs are not quantified in the insert, and new hires still need to learn NGL's own system, so the total expense cannot be stated.

Decision: NGL should choose on-the-job scanner training. It uses the known $650 saving per person, keeps the existing team under Priya Raman's direct control, and targets the 2.8% error at source. External recruitment is rejected because its cost is unquantified and it does not solve the training gap for the remaining staff; NGL can recruit later only if accuracy fails to improve after training. A further consideration is the 7.8% fall in online retail spending: with volumes under pressure, paying for external hires before accuracy improves would waste cash. Training the 14 existing staff protects the 75,000-consignment base and keeps the $650 per-person course fee as the only stated training cost. Priya Raman can monitor the 2.8% rate weekly to confirm the training works.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to NGL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of NGL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and uses the insert figures.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NGL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($17.50 − $10.00) = $300,000 ÷ $7.50 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 consignments a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $17.50 − $10.00 = $7.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NGL's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 40,000-unit break-even with 75,000 consignments: the margin of safety is 35,000 consignments, a buffer if the 7.8% fall in online retail spending reduces volumes.
2. Use the $7.50 contribution to test the $0.55 same-day premium: the $17.50 price can be modelled with the $10.00 variable cost held constant before retailers are offered a discount.
3. Check that 75,000 × $7.50 = $562,500 of contribution can cover $300,000 of fixed costs and service the $480,000 loan as the base rate reaches 5.35%.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $14.00 a consignment ($300,000 ÷ 75,000 + $10.00) against the 2.8% mis-sort rate and 5.2% returns to judge whether the new sorter is improving efficiency.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 35,000-unit margin of safety against weak online spending; $0.55 premium modelling on $17.50 and $10.00; $562,500 contribution to cover $300,000 fixed costs and the $480,000 loan; unit-cost benchmarking at $14.00 to tackle mis-sorting and returns.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NGL's profitability between 2024 and 2025. Has profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: The surplus after direct costs was $1,080,000 − $648,000 = $432,000 in 2024 and $1,260,000 − $693,000 = $567,000 in 2025. Operating return on sales used $108,000 ÷ $1,080,000 × 100 and $151,200 ÷ $1,260,000 × 100. Operating return on the capital base used $108,000 ÷ $720,000 × 100 and $151,200 ÷ $840,000 × 100. Revenue rose $180,000 while direct costs rose only $45,000.

Evaluation: All three indicators improved. The surplus share of sales rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, consistent with spreading warehouse costs over more consignments despite the 2.8% mis-sort rate. The operating share of sales rose from 10.0% to 12.0%, showing that overheads grew more slowly than revenue. Return on capital rose from 15.0% to 18.0% even though capital employed increased from $720,000 to $840,000, so the sorting investment is being used productively. Interest payable fell from $18,000 to $15,000, helping the result, but the 5.35% base rate may reverse that gain.

Conclusion: NGL's profitability has improved. The 40.0% to 45.0% surplus margin, 10.0% to 12.0% operating margin and 15.0% to 18.0% return on capital all confirm it. The strongest evidence is the rise in return on capital, because it shows that the larger capital base from the $840,000 programme is earning more rather than profit rising only because of higher sales. The 7.8% fall in online spending is a future risk rather than a 2025 result, so it does not change this conclusion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified improved judgement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NGL of offering guaranteed same-day delivery at the $0.55 premium supported by its survey.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 350 e-commerce retailers found 66% would pay $0.55 more for guaranteed same-day delivery, and 58% rank damage-free handling first. Charging the premium on top of the $17.50 price with the $10.00 variable cost unchanged raises contribution above $7.50 a consignment and strengthens the case for the $840,000 sorter. It also helps NGL win contracts from retailers worried about the 5.2% return rate.

Disadvantage: A guarantee is risky while 2.8% of parcels are mis-sorted and 33 complaints arrive each month. Missed same-day slots could trigger refunds or lost contracts, but the insert gives no penalty figures, so the net gain cannot be calculated. Meeting the promise may also need more vans than the $300,000 fixed-cost budget allows, especially if the 7.8% fall in online spending squeezes volume. NGL should check the 58% of retailers who rank damage-free handling first before committing to the promise.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NGL's survey, service record and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.35%, the 2.4% rise in fuel and warehouse electricity prices and the 7.8% fall in online retail consumer spending will affect NGL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise (4.6% to 5.35%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If the $480,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the added interest is 0.0075 × $480,000 = $3,600 a year, small against $300,000 of fixed costs, and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates could still make later borrowing for the van fleet dearer, but NGL can cap this by fixing the rate.

Fuel and warehouse electricity prices (up 2.4%): The insert gives one $10.00 variable cost and does not break it into components, so only an upper bound is defensible. If the whole $10.00 rose 2.4%, that adds 0.024 × $10.00 = $0.24 a consignment, or $18,000 a year at 75,000 consignments (75,000 × $0.24), trimming contribution from $7.50 toward $7.26. The effect is modest because the stated rise is small.

Online retail spending (down 7.8%): The insert does not state how spending links to NGL's volumes, so an illustrative bound is the honest approach. If consignments fell in line with the 7.8% fall, that is 0.078 × 75,000 = 5,850 fewer consignments, each carrying $7.50 of contribution, a $43,875 reduction. Retailers cutting stock orders would also make the 93.5% on-time target easier but revenue harder.

Conclusion: The 7.8% fall in online retail spending will have the greatest impact. Its illustrative $43,875 contribution loss exceeds the $18,000 upper-bound energy effect and the conditional $3,600 interest effect, and it threatens the 75,000-consignment volume needed to cover fixed costs. NGL should defend contracts with its $0.55 same-day offer rather than rely on cost savings.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to NGL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on NGL's volume, costs or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes using derivations shown from insert figures, with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the other two.
